steps.body: Try 52 − 27: the ones spot has 2 but must give 7 — it's short! The trading post runs **downhill**: break 1 ten into 10 ones. Now 52 is 4 tens and 12 ones (still 52). "Borrowing" is a misleading name — nothing gets paid back. It's a trade.
Watch the down-trade rescue the ones.

panels.title: The ones are short
panels.body: Ones first: 2 must give 7. Can't — the spot is 5 short. Subtraction stalls until the ones get reinforcements.

panels.title: Trade down
panels.body: One of the 5 tens breaks into 10 ones. Now: 4 tens, 12 ones — count it: 40 + 12 = 52. Same number, new packaging.

panels.title: Now subtract
panels.body: Ones: 12 − 7 = 5. Tens: 4 − 2 = 2. Answer: 25. The crossed-out 5-becomes-4 is the trade's paper trail.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the rescue arrives in the next panel.
widget.successFeedback: Short spot → trade down → subtract. 52 − 27 = 25, and nothing was 'borrowed' — it was repackaged.

predict.prompt: Trading a ten for ones in 52 — does that change the VALUE of 52?
predict.reveal: 4 tens and 12 ones weigh exactly what 5 tens and 2 ones did — the trade rearranges, never adds or removes. That conservation is what makes borrowing legal.

steps.body: What actually moved in that trade?
explanationVariants: A whole TEN moved — and became ten ONES on arrival. 63 repackaged as 5 tens + 13 ones is still 50 + 13 = 63.
The crossed-out 6→5 and the new 13 are two halves of one trade: one ten left the tens, ten ones arrived in the ones.

widget.prompt: In 63 − 38, the 6 becomes a 5 and the 3 becomes 13. What happened?

options.label: One ten traded down into 10 ones — 63 repackaged as 5 tens, 13 ones
options.feedback: Check the value: 50 + 13 = 63. The trade changed the packaging, never the amount.

options.label: A 1 was moved from the 6 over to the 3
options.feedback: It LOOKS like a little 1 hopped over — but a whole TEN moved, and it became ten ones on landing. That's why 3 jumps all the way to 13, not 4.

options.label: The 6 shrank because subtraction shrinks things
options.feedback: The 6 shrank because it PAID for the trade — one of its tens broke into ones. Subtraction itself hasn't even started yet.

options.label: It's a mistake — 63 became 53
options.feedback: Count all of it: 5 tens (50) plus 13 ones = 63 exactly. The repackaged number is untouched.

steps.body: Now the boss level: **305 − 128**. The ones are short, but the tens spot is EMPTY — a zero can't lend anything. So chain the trade: break a hundred into 10 tens FIRST, then break one of those tens into ones. 305 becomes 2 hundreds, 9 tens, 15 ones — still 305.
The everyday trade, start to finish.
explanationVariants: Trade: 4 tens, 12 ones. Then 12 − 7 = 5 and 4 − 2 = 2: answer 25.
Guard it: 52 − 27 ≈ 50 − 30 = 20, and 25 sits right beside the guard.

widget.prompt: 52 − 27 = ? Tap each column to work it out; tap a top digit to break a ten when you need one.

commonResults.feedback: 35 flipped the ones — it computed 7 − 2 because 2 − 7 'doesn't work.' The fix isn't flipping; it's trading a ten down so the ones CAN pay: 12 − 7.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Ones short → break a ten (4 tens, 12 ones) → subtract each spot.
widget.successFeedback: 52 − 27 = 25: break a ten so the ones read 12 − 7, then 4 − 2 in the tens.

steps.body: The chain trade, assembled in order.

widget.prompt: Put the steps of 305 − 128 in working order.

items.label: Break a ten: 2 hundreds, 9 tens, 15 ones
Break a hundred: 2 hundreds, 10 tens, 5 ones

misorderFeedback.feedback: Subtracting jumped ahead of the trades — but the ones are still short (5 can't give 8). Open the trading post first.
You can't break a ten yet — the tens spot is EMPTY (0). The hundred must break first to stock the tens.

widget.missFeedback: The zero forces a chain: hundred breaks into tens, THEN a ten breaks into ones, THEN subtract.

explanationVariants: Chain: 2 hundreds, 9 tens, 15 ones. Then 15 − 8 = 7, 9 − 2 = 7, 2 − 1 = 1: answer 177.
Guard: 305 − 128 ≈ 300 − 100 = 200, and 177 lives near the guard.

commonErrors.feedback: 223 flipped every short spot (8−5, 2−0, keeping 3−1) — the smaller-from-larger shortcut. Short spots trade down instead; they never flip.
187 broke the hundred but forgot the second break — the tens must ALSO lend one to the ones, leaving 9 tens, not 10.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Two breaks (hundred → tens, then ten → ones), then subtract spot by spot.

hints: 400 − 156 crosses TWO zeros — chain the trades from the hundreds.
400 repackages as 3 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones; subtract to get 244.
Then 44 chairs come BACK — they rejoin the count.
explanationVariants: Guard step 1: 400 − 156 ≈ 400 − 200 = 200; 244 fits. Then the return adds 44: 288.

widget.prompt: A school has 400 chairs. 156 are taken to the gym. Later, 44 are brought back. How many chairs does the school have outside the gym now?

commonErrors.feedback: 244 is after the gym takes its chairs — step one done! But 44 of them come BACK. Add the returns.
200 SUBTRACTED the returning 44 — but returning chairs rejoin the pile. The second step adds.
356 is 400 − 44 — the gym's 156 never left! Two moves happen in order: −156 first, then +44.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Two moves: the chain-trade subtraction 400 − 156, then add the 44 that return.

steps.body: No zero can stall your subtraction now.
takeaways: A short spot trades down: one ten becomes ten ones (value unchanged).
Across a zero, chain it: hundred → tens first, then ten → ones.
Never flip to smaller-from-larger — short spots trade, they don't surrender.
steps.teaser: one last habit locks it all in: guard every answer with an estimate.

concept.body: Quick rewind. When a spot is short, **break a ten**: 31 − 15 → the ones (1) can't give 5, so 31 repackages as 2 tens, 11 ones. Now 11 − 5 = 6 and 2 − 1 = 1: answer 16. Short spot? Trade down. Never flip the digits.

explanationVariants: Trade: 3 tens, 12 ones. Then 12 − 8 = 4 and 3 − 1 = 2: answer 24.

options.feedback: One trade (3 tens, 12 ones), then 12 − 8 = 4 and 3 − 1 = 2.
36 flipped the ones (8 − 2) instead of trading. The 2 is short — break a ten so it can pay: 12 − 8.
34 traded the ones correctly but forgot the tens paid for it — after the trade only 3 tens remain: 3 − 1 = 2.
